analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 and then adjusts it each year with inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate's labor committee since June 2025 with no vote and no movement, despite a Republican sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the federal minimum wage law so that every covered worker must be paid at least $15 an hour, starting the January 1 after the bill becomes law. After that, the wage would rise automatically each year with inflation, so Congress would not have to keep passing new increases. The bill was introduced by Senator Josh Hawley, a Republican, with support from Democratic senators, and was sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, where it has stayed.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid less than $15 an hour — roughly millions of people in fast food, retail, care work, hospitality, and other low-wage jobs — would get an immediate raise, and the automatic inflation adjustment would protect that raise from being eroded over time.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes a $15 federal minimum into the Fair Labor Standards Act, effective January 1 of the first year after enactment, replacing the current $7.25 floor that has not changed since 2009.

Beginning the second year after enactment, and every year after, the minimum wage automatically rises by the increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, so the wage keeps pace with living costs without further action by Congress.
The Secretary of Labor is directed to calculate and publish the annual inflation adjustment each September 30, rounded to the nearest five cents.

analysis.who_pays: The employers of minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail stores, hotels, franchises, and small businesses with large low-wage workforces — would bear higher payroll costs, some portion of which may be passed to consumers through prices. Taxpayers also indirectly benefit, since fewer low-wage workers rely on public assistance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers like restaurants and retail

drawbacks.text: A $15 federal floor applies the same wage to high-cost cities and low-cost rural areas alike, and the burden falls on employers in low-wage industries; many small businesses would face sharply higher payroll costs overnight when the floor takes effect.

Economists debate how many jobs a steep minimum wage increase eliminates; studies of past increases find effects ranging from negligible to modest job losses among the least experienced workers, and a one-step jump to $15 is much larger than increases states have typically phased in gradually.
The bill contains no small-business phase-in or tip-credit carve-out, so restaurants and franchises currently using the lower tip minimum wage would have to move straight to the full floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and large for the lowest-paid workers: an immediate raise of more than double the current federal floor, plus automatic inflation protection. The cost falls on specific employers rather than the public budget, but a steep national jump with no phase-in for small businesses or tipped workers is a real and legitimate objection, and some job loss among entry-level workers is possible even under favorable estimates. On balance, this is a straightforward transfer from employers of low-wage labor to low-wage workers, and the inflation indexing makes the gains durable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and has not had a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on June 10, 2025, joined by Senator Peter Welch and one other Democratic cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — has been recorded in the committee since referral, and the Congress remains in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers who pay below $15 an hour are better off, since the bill has stalled and the current $7.25 federal floor remains in effect.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put his name on a $15 minimum wage with automatic inflation indexing.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 10, 2025 and has taken no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — in the months since.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican lead sponsor with Democratic cosponsors — but with no vote yet, there is no record of how either party's members would line up.

industries.note: Restaurants are the largest employers of minimum-wage and tipped workers, so a $15 floor directly raises their labor costs. Their interest in keeping the wage low runs against the raise their own employees would get.
Big-box stores and franchise chains with large hourly workforces would face higher payroll costs, though many large chains already pay above $15 in practice.
Hotels and lodging employ many low-wage housekeeping and service staff who would get raises, while the industry's labor costs rise; there is no tip-credit carve-out in the bill.
Small employers in low-cost areas face the sharpest cost jump since the bill has no phase-in or small-business exception, while their low-wage employees gain directly.

analysis.trajectory: Most minimum wage bills die quietly in committee, and this one has shown no committee activity since referral. The committee is chaired by a senator of the sponsor's own party, which could in theory help, but no hearing has been scheduled and the bill has only two Democratic cosponsors. The most likely path is that it sits without action for the rest of this Congress unless leadership elevates it or a broader wage bill absorbs its provisions.
